clue.text: If writer runs during play, kid gets excited

parts.note: R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs

indicators.note: letters that get excited jump about and land out of order

parts.note: taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A child gets worked up when a batsman scores runs during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: "If" looks like the start of a conditional sentence, but it is the title of Kipling's famous poem, so "If writer" means the author of If.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by work: the author is identified through his best-known poem, If, a British favourite.

clue.text: Hunt film role in production that's basic

indicators.note: a production reworks its material into a new shape

parts.note: taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: An actor's part in a Hunt film turns out to be a rather ordinary one.
explanation.walkthrough: "Hunt" suggests the actor Helen Hunt or Ethan Hunt of Mission: Impossible, but it is only four letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Run-of-the-mill means ordinary or basic, with nothing special added.

clue.text: In central Madrid, crowds stunned to find swamp

indicators.note: asks for the letters at the centre of each of the next three words

parts.note: the middle two of six letters
the middle two of six letters
the middle letter of seven

explanation.surface: In the heart of Madrid, spectators are left stunned.
explanation.walkthrough: "swamp" reads as a noun, a marsh, but it is the verb: to flood or overwhelm.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: both mean to flood or overwhelm, whether with water or with too much work.

clue.text: Happen to come across sum left for old teacher

parts.note: things that arise happen
to tot up is to add, and a tot is a sum
the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles on a sum of money that was left to an old schoolmaster.
explanation.walkthrough: "Happen to come across" reads as one phrase meaning stumble upon; it splits into ARISE and a container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle was an ancient Greek philosopher who taught Alexander the Great.

clue.text: One coming out with lace undone — it's a fiasco

parts.note: a deb, or debutante, is a young woman coming out into society

indicators.note: undone lace comes loose and its letters fall out of order

parts.note: taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A debutante makes her entrance with her lace coming apart, and it is a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: A debutante was a young upper-class woman formally presented, or "coming out", at a society ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns name a sudden, humiliating collapse of a plan or event.

clue.text: Urinals at sea are somewhat narrow, perhaps

indicators.note: things at sea are adrift and confused

parts.note: taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: The toilets on board ship are a bit cramped.
explanation.walkthrough: "narrow" pulls toward cramped space, but here it means narrow-minded; "perhaps" admits the definition is a loose one.
explanation.definitionFit: Insular people are inward-looking and rather narrow-minded, like islanders cut off from the world.

clue.text: Enticed by reports of miraculous site

indicators.note: a report is something spoken and heard

parts.note: Lourdes, the French shrine of healing miracles, is said "loord"

explanation.surface: Pilgrims drawn in by stories of a place where miracles happen.
explanation.walkthrough: Lourdes is a pilgrimage town in France famous for reported miraculous cures; in English it is pronounced like "lured".
explanation.definitionFit: Lured and enticed both mean tempted into coming.

clue.text: Food I turn into stew …

indicators.note: a stew is a mixture with everything jumbled together

parts.note: taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A cook turns some food into a stew.
explanation.walkthrough: "stew" looks like the dish the food becomes, but it is the instruction to mix up "I turn into"; "turn" also tempts as an indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutrition is nourishment, the food a body takes in.

clue.text: Girl is initially nervous about old man's intentions

indicators.note: points to the initial letter of each following word

parts.note: the first letters of the five words

explanation.surface: A young woman is uneasy about what an older man has in mind.
explanation.walkthrough: "initially" seems to apply only to "nervous" (as in at first), but it takes the first letter of every word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: "Girl" in crosswords often stands for any female first name, and this one comes from the Book of Ruth.

clue.text: Interest Spooner expressed in career inducement

indicators.note: the Rev Spooner swapped the first sounds of words

parts.note: to career is to race along; it takes the B sound from the next word
bait is an inducement; it takes the R sound from the word before

explanation.surface: Spooner tells a job-seeker about a perk offered to lure them.
explanation.walkthrough: "career" looks like a noun, a job, but it is the verb to rush, giving RACE.
explanation.definitionFit: The base rate is the central bank's benchmark interest rate.

clue.text: … giving rich, full taste of Europe

definitions.text: giving rich, full taste of Europe

parts.note: after the ellipsis this reads as more about the food of 7 Down: a rich, full flavour
the taste is really a long sampling of a whole continent, the trip young aristocrats once took to finish their education

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from 7 Down, the food that gives a rich, full taste; here the taste is of a whole continent. The Grand Tour was the long journey through Europe that wealthy young Britons made to finish their education.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grand Tour gave rich young travellers a full taste of Europe's cities and culture.

clue.text: Encourage a jerk to become extremist

parts.note: to fan flames or hopes is to encourage them
as printed
a tic is an involuntary jerk

explanation.surface: Egging on an idiot until he turns radical.
explanation.walkthrough: "jerk" reads as a fool, but it means a twitch.
explanation.definitionFit: A fanatic holds extreme, uncompromising views.

clue.text: Woman drops young hunk for being somewhat rowdy

parts.note: a lady is a woman
the first letter of young
a dish is an attractive person

explanation.surface: A woman dumps her young boyfriend because he is a bit loutish.
explanation.walkthrough: "drops young hunk" reads as dumping a boyfriend; it actually removes Y and leaves the hunk to supply DISH.
explanation.definitionFit: Laddish behaviour is boisterous and a bit yobbish, typical of young men out together.

clue.text: Son in pain? He made sure it was all over!

definitions.text: He made sure it was all over!

parts.note: hurt is pain
the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: A suffering son, and someone who ensured the game was finished.
explanation.walkthrough: Geoff Hurst scored England's last goal in the 1966 football World Cup final as the commentator said "They think it's all over... it is now!"
explanation.definitionFit: Hurst's hat-trick goal sealed the 1966 final, making sure it really was all over.

clue.text: One standing by as church abandons service during break …

parts.note: a rest is a break
as printed
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A churchgoer hangs around as the congregation walks out of a service during a break.
explanation.walkthrough: "abandons" makes the church the thing leaving, but it is the church's letters that leave the service; CE is the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A reservist is a reserve soldier standing by to be called up.

clue.text: Land fish, one that's out of this world?

definitions.text: one that's out of this world?

parts.note: earth is land
the ling is a sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: Landing a fish so strange it seems alien.
explanation.walkthrough: "out of this world" usually means amazing or alien; read literally, an earthling comes out of, that is from, this world.
explanation.definitionFit: An earthling is a native of Earth, one who hails from this world; the question mark flags the twist.

clue.text: … which may not be what it sounds like

definitions.text: which may not be what it sounds like

parts.note: after the ellipsis this looks like a comment on the reservist of 14 Down
read literally: a word that sounds identical to another word but is not that word

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins it to 14 Down, but it stands alone. A homophone sounds like another word yet is not that word, so it is literally not what it sounds like.
explanation.definitionFit: A homophone has the sound of a different word with a different meaning or spelling.

clue.text: One of three getting name checked in Great Hosannah

parts.note: a member of a famous literary trio
a name, ATHOS, is literally found inside greAT HOSannah

explanation.surface: One of a trio gets a mention in a great cry of praise.
explanation.walkthrough: The name ATHOS, one of Dumas's Three Musketeers, sits inside "greAT HOSannah", so he is literally name-checked there.
explanation.definitionFit: Athos, Porthos and Aramis are the three musketeers of Dumas's novel.

clue.text: Partial text remains source for mathematical values

indicators.note: only part of the text is wanted

parts.note: sits inside tEXT REMAins

explanation.surface: A fragment of an old manuscript is where some mathematical figures came from.
explanation.walkthrough: "remains" looks like the main verb; it only supplies the last four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Extrema are the maximum and minimum values of a mathematical function.

clue.text: Ruled measure government introduced must be reversed

indicators.note: the result is to be turned back to front

parts.note: denier is a unit measuring how fine a yarn is, as in 15-denier tights
the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: A ruled-on measure the government brought in has to be overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: "Ruled" first reads as an adjective describing the measure, but it is the definition, the past tense of rule.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: both describe a sovereign holding power over a realm.

clue.text: Group for the clever chaps observed losing weight

parts.note: chaps are men

indicators.note: losing weight is read literally: the word for observed sheds the letter standing for weight

parts.note: saw means observed
the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: Clever blokes in a slimming club were seen shedding pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: "the clever chaps" looks like one unit; the definition stops at "clever", and chaps is MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Mensa is the society whose members must score highly on an IQ test.

clue.text: There's nothing bigger in case containing plastic rag

parts.note: lest means in case, as in 'lest we forget'

indicators.note: plastic material can be moulded into a new shape

parts.note: taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: No bigger plastic bag holds a cleaning cloth than this case.
explanation.walkthrough: "plastic rag" suggests a material, but plastic is the anagram signal and "in case" is one unit, LEST.
explanation.definitionFit: If something is the largest, there is nothing bigger than it.

clue.text: Poles sounding out German city

indicators.note: sounding out means saying the letters aloud

parts.note: the south and north poles, abbreviated S and N, spoken as letter names

explanation.surface: Polish people exploring a city in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: "Poles" reads as Polish people, but it is the magnetic poles S and N.
explanation.definitionFit: Essen is an industrial city in western Germany.

clue.text: Appropriate for poet to admit who he is

parts.note: introducing himself he says "I'm"
Ezra Pound, the American poet

explanation.surface: Is it fitting for a poet to confess his identity?
explanation.walkthrough: "Appropriate" looks like the adjective meaning fitting, but it is the verb to seize.
explanation.definitionFit: To impound goods is to appropriate them, taking them into custody.

clue.text: Aunt's theory is occasionally thorough

indicators.note: only now and then, every other letter

parts.note: the even letters of aUnT'S tHeOrY

explanation.surface: Auntie's pet theory turns out to be pretty rigorous now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: "thorough" is the adjective sense, as in an utter disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter and thorough both mean complete, as in an utter or thorough mess.

clue.text: He proved drug is the same; host agreed

definitions.text: He proved drug is the same; host agreed

parts.note: a scientist famous for one result

parts.words: drug is the same; host agreed
parts.note: read as symbols: E (the drug ecstasy) = (is the same as) MC (host) squared (agreed, as in settled)

explanation.surface: A scientist shows that a drug is unchanged, and the presenter concurs.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as symbols: drug is E (ecstasy), "is the same" is an equals sign, host is MC and agreed is "squared" (settled), so the clue spells E = MC², the equation he is famous for.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Einstein derived E = mc², that energy equals mass times the speed of light squared.

clue.text: United involved in nil-nil draw? That's better

parts.note: nil is zero, shaped like O
UTD is the usual abbreviation in football club names
the second zero
surface padding that completes the football score

explanation.surface: A football fan relieved that United at least got a goalless draw.
explanation.walkthrough: "draw" only completes the football picture of a nil-nil score; "better" is the verb, to surpass.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: both mean to surpass a rival's performance.

clue.text: Champion branded Sartre a drunk

indicators.note: a drunk staggers, and so do these letters

parts.note: taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A champion of a cause calls the philosopher Sartre a drunkard.
explanation.walkthrough: "branded" looks like the verb of an accusation, but it is just seven letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: the soldier who carried the flag became a word for anyone leading and championing a cause.
